extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, literary students and critics studying Aristotle's Poetics / how to compose tragic and epic fables
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing tragic and epic fables based on Aristotelian principles: how to shape a single unified action, use probability/necessity, handle names and invention, and elicit pity and terror. Useful for playwrights, epic poets, and students of dramatic theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of the Action (single, entire action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy (and epic) ought to be the imitation of one entire Action — a single whole Action that has a beginning, middle, and end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All parts must be linked so that transposing or removing any part causes a sensible change or destroys the unity. If an Action is split (e.g., two revenges), its unity and the subject's identity are lost. Examples: the Iliad's unity would be destroyed if Achilles suddenly received satisfaction early; a single Action must be perfect and complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of Parts (members must be indispensable)
rubrics_metrics.description: What can be put in, or left out, without causing a sensible change cannot be part of the Action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the analogy of a body: a member that can be removed without perceptible alteration is not essential. This is a rule to distinguish true episodes from false/additional ones. Anti-pattern: histories like certain passages in Statius's Thebaids that add nothing to the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid epicodic/episodic fables (no foreign, unjoined episodes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodic (epicodick) fables are the most imperfect: they contain episodes not joined to others truly or probably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and excise foreign or superadded material that does not contribute causally to the principal action. Such episodes can form separate, complete actions and so corrupt unity (example: the Theseus and Dirce episode in Oedipus considered a vicious episode).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet writes what might/ought to happen (truth or verisimilitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the property of the Poet to relate things just as they happened, but as they might or ought necessarily or probably to happen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet must follow necessity or probability rather than literal historical fact. He is master of his subject and may alter events to produce an artful causal sequence and the proper form (beginning, middle, end).

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between Poet and Historian
rubrics_metrics.description: A historian writes what did happen; a poet writes what might or ought to have happened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not just verse vs prose: the essential difference lies in matter — poetry treats the general (what any person of such character would do), while history records particulars. Hence poetry is argued to be more philosophical/moral because it treats universals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality of Subjects (universality)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'general' thing is what every man of such a character necessarily or probably ought to say or do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing characters like Achilles, aim for universal/representative behavior so the action instructs broadly. The poet's aim is to depict what people of a given character would do under those circumstances, not merely to recount unique particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as author/master of subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet ought to be the author of his subject as much as of his verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet has liberty to dispose and order incidents (even real ones) to ensure probability and causal connection. Being the 'poet' implies mastery of the subject/fable — not merely ornamenting preexisting facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of names: invented vs true
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets may invent names and things, and often do; tragic poets also employ true names for plausibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invented names/subjects are permissible and can please (example: Agathon's play called 'The Flower'). True names lend credibility and allow use of historical adventures as plausible material; one or two known names are often sufficient while other elements can be invented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known subjects safer but invention allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary always to tie oneself scrupulously to known fables; known subjects are ordinarily safer though invented ones can succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace cautions Romans that invented subjects are harder to manage, but Greeks succeeded with invention. Choose known subjects when inexperienced; experiment with invention when you can render generality and probability convincingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and Necessity over Accident
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must follow necessity or probability; mere accidental events (without causal design) do not produce the intended effects in tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on chance-caused surprises (e.g., a man crushed by a falling house) — surprise must arise from causes and an artful causal chain so events appear designed rather than purely fortuitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise as necessary to Tragedy (source of pity and terror)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy imitates such an action as excites terror and compassion; these passions come by surprise when some things are produced from others contrary to expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design fables so that the wonderful or surprising result flows from a causal progression (not random chance). The statue of Mytys (falling and killing his murderer seemingly by design) exemplifies a non-accidental surprise that elicits terror and compassion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy's proper emotions: pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy aims to excite primarily terror and compassion (pity); other passions like admiration are not the proper end of tragic refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a play seeks to refine the audience by admiration rather than pity/fear, it strays from the essence of tragedy (example: Nicomedes' admiring courage creating admiration rather than pity/fear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make causes and motives visible (causal linkage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should lay open the causes and effects of incidents so that the first incident becomes the cause of the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because poets control their matter, they must supply convincing motives/causes to bind incidents; history rarely explains causes, but poetic action must make causal chains intelligible to produce necessity/probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pandering to actors/performers (complaisance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets' complaisance to actors (or companies) — adding material to let particular actors 'appear' or shine — can force the breaking of unity by introducing episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist inserting episodes or stretching subjects to accommodate performers or theatrical rivalries; these compromises often corrupt the unity and quality of the fable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy vs Satyrical poetry (general vs particular)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic poets commonly invent subjects and names and keep to generality; satyrical (iambic) poets confine themselves to particulars and personal attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand genre differences: comedy freely invents and allegorizes to depict manners; satyrical verse targets particulars and real persons (anti-pattern for general poetic universality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whatever is possible is credible (plausibility principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: That which is possible (or has occurred) is credible; what has happened demonstrates possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plausibility to persuade the audience: employing known names or incidents can increase credibility because listeners accept that such events could occur — this is a tool to ground invented fables.
